questions.q: Proper use of lubricants cannot reduce —

The physical quantity equal to the change in momentum of a body is —
A ball of mass m strikes a rigid wall with speed u and rebounds with the same speed. The impulse imparted by the wall is —
questions.work: Taking the rebound direction as positive: Δp = mu − (−mu) = 2mu.

questions.q: When a constant net external force acts on a body, which quantity does not change?
Which of the following is always in the direction of the net external force on a body?

A block just starts sliding when the inclined plane makes 30° with the vertical. The coefficient of friction is —
questions.work:
30° with the vertical means the incline is at 60° to the horizontal.
At the point of sliding μ = tan θ = tan 60° = √3.

A constant force of 10 N acts on a 2.5 kg body at rest for 2 s. Its velocity after 3 s is —
questions.work:
a = F/m = 10/2.5 = 4 m/s²; after 2 s, v = 4 × 2 = 8 m/s.

sections.title: Objective type questions: each has two parts of 1 mark (fill in the blanks, true/false, match or one word).

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: (a) ______ is the weakest force in nature. (b) A gun recoils after firing to conserve ______.
Match: (a) Law of conservation of linear momentum — ? (b) Expression for friction force — ? [f = μN / F = ma / p_total = constant]
Fill in the blanks: (a) Mass is a measure of ______. (b) Impulse equals the area under the ______–time graph.
State True or False: (a) Action and reaction act on the same body and cancel. (b) Rolling friction is less than sliding friction.
questions.answer:
(a) False — they act on different bodies.
(b) True.

questions.q: Complete: (a) 50 N opposes a 10 kg body moving at 10 m/s; deceleration = ______. (b) Time to stop = ______.
Fill in the blanks: (a) A lift falls freely; the apparent weight of a person in it is ______. (b) The angle of the incline at which a block just slides is the angle of ______.

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: Why are passengers thrown forward when a speeding bus stops suddenly?
questions.answer: The lower body stops with the bus, but the upper body tends to keep moving forward because of inertia of motion, so passengers lurch forward.

or.q: Why do passengers fall backward when a bus suddenly starts from rest?
or.answer: The feet move forward with the bus, but the upper body tends to stay at rest because of inertia of rest, so passengers fall backward.

questions.q: A ball of mass m is thrown up with speed v and returns to the thrower with the same speed. Find the change in its momentum.
questions.answer:
Initial momentum = mv upward; final = mv downward.
Taking up as positive: Δp = (−mv) − (mv) = −2mv, i.e. 2mv downward. The magnitude of momentum is unchanged.

or.q: Identify the action–reaction forces on a book lying on a table.
or.answer: The book pushes down on the table with a force equal to its weight (action); the table pushes up on the book with an equal force (reaction). They act on different bodies.

questions.q: Mention two ways of reducing friction between surfaces.
questions.answer: (1) Using lubricants such as oil or grease. (2) Using ball bearings or rollers, since rolling friction is much smaller. Polishing and streamlining also help.

or.q: Give two examples of conservation of linear momentum.
or.answer: (1) Recoil of a gun when a bullet is fired. (2) Rocket propulsion — gases thrown back push the rocket forward. (Also a boat moving back as a person jumps off.)

questions.q: Why does a cricketer draw his hands back while catching a fast ball?
questions.answer: Drawing the hands back increases the time in which the ball's momentum is reduced to zero. Since F = Δp/t, the force on the hands is smaller and they are not hurt.

questions.q: Show that the momentum of a particle is unchanged if the force on it is zero.
questions.answer: F = dp/dt. If F = 0 then dp/dt = 0, so p is constant: the particle keeps the same momentum (first law).

questions.q: Define the coefficients of static and kinetic friction.
questions.answer:
μs = limiting (maximum) static friction ÷ normal reaction, when the body is just about to slide.
μk = kinetic friction ÷ normal reaction, when the body is sliding. Usually μk < μs.

questions.q: A 50 kg woman is in a lift moving up with acceleration 5 m/s². What does the weighing machine record? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.answer: R − mg = ma ⇒ R = m(g + a) = 50 × 15 = 750 N (about 75 kg wt).

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: Two masses of 2 kg and 3 kg hang from a light string over a frictionless pulley. Find the acceleration and the tension. (g = 9.8 m/s²)
questions.answer:
a = (m₂ − m₁)g/(m₁ + m₂) = (3 − 2) × 9.8/5 = 1.96 m/s².
T = 2m₁m₂g/(m₁ + m₂) = 2 × 2 × 3 × 9.8/5 = 23.5 N.
The 3 kg mass moves down and the 2 kg mass moves up.

questions.q: A 1 kg body at rest explodes into three pieces of masses in the ratio 1 : 1 : 3. The two equal pieces fly off at right angles, each at 30 m/s. Find the velocity of the heavier piece.
questions.answer:
Masses: 0.2 kg, 0.2 kg and 0.6 kg.
Momenta of the light pieces: 0.2 × 30 = 6 kg m/s each, at right angles; resultant = 6√2 kg m/s.
The total momentum is zero, so the heavy piece has 6√2 kg m/s in the opposite direction.
v = 6√2/0.6 = 10√2 ≈ 14.1 m/s, at 135° to each light piece.

or.q: How is the impulse of a force found when the force is (a) constant and (b) variable?
or.answer:
(a) Constant force: impulse = F × t = change in momentum.
(b) Variable force: impulse = area under the force–time graph (∫F dt), still equal to the change in momentum.

questions.q: Four equal blocks of mass m tied by strings on a smooth floor are pulled by a force F. Find the tensions T₁, T₂, T₃ (T₁ nearest the force).
questions.answer:
Acceleration of the system a = F/4m.
T₁ pulls three blocks: T₁ = 3m × a = 3F/4.
T₂ pulls two blocks: T₂ = 2m × a = F/2.
T₃ pulls one block: T₃ = m × a = F/4.

questions.q: State Newton's second law. Derive F = ma and define the newton.
questions.answer:
Law: the rate of change of momentum is proportional to the net force and in its direction.
F ∝ dp/dt = d(mv)/dt = m dv/dt = ma (mass constant). With the SI unit chosen so that the constant is 1, F = ma.
1 newton is the force that gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s².

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: State and prove the law of conservation of linear momentum using Newton's third law. Aman (60 kg) moves at 1 m/s towards Manoj (40 kg), who moves at 1.5 m/s towards Aman. Find their momenta.
questions.answer:
Law: if no net external force acts on a system, its total momentum stays constant.
Proof: bodies A and B collide for time t. By the third law F_AB = −F_BA, so F_AB t = −F_BA t, i.e. Δp_A = −Δp_B. Hence Δp_A + Δp_B = 0, so m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂.
Aman: p = 60 × 1 = 60 kg m/s. Manoj: p = 40 × 1.5 = 60 kg m/s in the opposite direction. Total momentum = 60 − 60 = 0.

or.q: State and prove Newton's second law. A 0.4 kg ball rolling at 20 m/s comes to rest in 10 s. Find the (constant) force stopping it.
or.answer:
Second law: F = dp/dt; for constant mass F = m dv/dt = ma.
Ball: a = (v − u)/t = (0 − 20)/10 = −2 m/s².
F = ma = 0.4 × (−2) = −0.8 N, i.e. 0.8 N opposite to the motion.

questions.q: State Newton's three laws of motion. Use the first law to define force and inertia and the second law to define acceleration.
questions.answer:
First law: a body stays at rest or in uniform motion in a straight line unless an external force acts on it. So force is what changes a body's state of rest or motion, and inertia is a body's tendency to resist such a change (measured by mass).
Second law: the rate of change of momentum equals the net force, F = ma. So acceleration is the rate of change of velocity produced by a net force, a = F/m.
Third law: to every action there is an equal and opposite reaction, acting on different bodies.

questions.q: In each case name the forces acting and explain why the net force is zero: (i) a raindrop falling at constant speed; (ii) a cork floating on water; (iii) a kite held stationary; (iv) a car moving at constant velocity on a rough road; (v) a fast electron in force-free space.
questions.answer:
(i) Weight down is balanced by air resistance (viscous drag) and buoyancy up — constant velocity, so net force zero.
(ii) Weight down equals the buoyant force up.
(iii) Weight and string tension are balanced by the force of the wind on the kite.
(iv) The engine's forward force on the car (through the road) equals friction and air resistance.
(v) No force acts at all.
In every case there is no acceleration, so by the second law the net force is zero.
